sections.h2: What sets Florissant apart as a place to sell a house?
sections.html:
Florissant is a second-ring suburb north of St. Louis and the biggest municipality in its county. Much of its housing went up in the postwar boom, and that age profile drives what buyers and inspectors ask about.

French settlers farmed the valley in the 1780s, and the first civilian government formed in 1786. The Spanish census of 1787 counted 40 people and seven plantations. The village was called St. Ferdinand under Spanish rule, and the city went by that name again from 1857 to 1939. Census counts tell the rest of the story: 3,737 residents in 1950, 38,166 in 1960 and 65,908 in 1970, as developers turned farmland into subdivisions. Roughly 18,000 houses were built between 1947 and 1980.

Today the city covers 12.55 square miles of land. Most of it lies north of I-270, with the Missouri River along the northwest edge, where the city keeps the 108-acre Sunset Park. Hazelwood and Ferguson sit to the south, Black Jack to the east and Old Jamestown to the north.

  • Old Town is a locally designated historic district created by ordinance in 1969.
  • The St. Ferdinand Central Historic District in Old Town carries a National Register listing.
  • The 2020 count was 52,533 residents, and the latest federal estimate is 51,124.

sections.h2: How do Florissant's housing numbers compare with the rest of the county?
sections.html:
Florissant leans toward owners and moderate prices, so a seller here is usually pricing against other mid-century houses on similar lots. About two of every three households own, and 89.6% of residents lived in the same house a year earlier.

The 2020 census recorded 22,710 housing units in Florissant, with 6.7% vacant. Empty rentals made up 9.6% of that stock, against 1.8% for owner homes. Rent of $1,288 a month runs above the $1,235 that owners with a mortgage report paying.

sections.h2: Does Florissant require an inspection before a house changes hands?
sections.html:
No. According to the city's occupancy inspection page, a Florissant property can be sold as-is without an inspection, and the buyer then has to obtain and pay for the inspection and the occupancy permit before anyone moves in.

The city built its minimum standards around cooking, heating and sanitary equipment, light and ventilation, and upkeep of existing buildings. Those are the items an inspector walks through. The city also notes that its report can differ from a private inspector or an FHA or VA appraisal, and it suggests buyers use the results from every source instead of pitting one report against another. A seller who knows the roof, furnace, water heater, electrical panel and plumbing stack are in working order has fewer surprises during that final walk-through.

One city program can affect timing. Florissant's Home Improvement Program offers a no-interest forgivable loan of up to $7,000 for safety and code repairs, secured by a deed of trust. If the owner sells, rents or transfers the home within five years, the loan must be repaid, and for a sale it is paid at closing. The 2026 application window was set for May 1 to May 8, 2026, so it has closed for this year. If you took a loan in the past five years, call Community Development at 314-839-7680 and get the balance in writing before you sign a contract.

  • Public Works and the Building Division handle occupancy permits and inspections.
  • Commercial buildings, including schools and churches, need their own occupancy inspection and permit before use.
  • The Permit Portal at my.florissantmo.com takes business license and commercial occupancy applications.

sections.h2: What will the recorder and the collector charge on a Florissant sale?
sections.html:
The Recorder of Deeds charges $26 for page one of a standard deed and $3 for every page after it. A $25 non-standard fee applies if the document does not meet the Missouri Document Formatting Standards, and eRecording vendors may add their own charges. The office is at 41 S Central Ave in Clayton, and originals go by mail or drop-off with a check or money order payable to ROD.

The county Collector of Revenue sends the real estate tax bill. Payment or postmark must land on or before the last day of December. Later payments carry up to 18% interest per year plus a 2% penalty under RSMo chapters 139 and 140. Your title agent can show how the year's bill gets divided at the closing table.

If you think the Assessor valued your house too high, the independent Board of Equalization hears appeals filed between May 1 and the second Monday of July. The 2026 cutoff was July 13, so it has passed. The Assessor must finalize the rolls by July 1, and after that only the Board can change a value. Keep photos, repair estimates and recent sales for next year.

  • Pull a paid-to-date statement from the Collector of Revenue before listing.
  • Ask your title company whether a Home Improvement Program lien needs a release.
  • Request a copy of your recorded deed from the Recorder of Deeds if you cannot find it.

sections.h2: Which ways of selling fit a Florissant house?
sections.html:
Your route should follow the shape the house is in and the date you need cash. Florissant's older ranch and split-level homes often carry aging mechanical systems, and that shows up in every path below.

  • A listing with an agent reaches the most shoppers. It also brings inspection requests, financing contingencies and the buyer's occupancy inspection.
  • An as-is cash sale suits an owner who would rather skip showings and repairs. The purchaser then takes on the city occupancy process.
  • Selling on your own avoids an agent's fee and keeps pricing, paperwork and negotiation in your hands.

Whichever route you pick, compare the net amount after tax proration, any lien payoff, title charges and deed recording. A higher headline price can leave less in your pocket than a lower offer with fewer conditions. Ask each buyer how long closing takes and whether they pay recording costs.

sections.h2: Which schools and landmarks shape buyer interest in Florissant?
sections.html:
Florissant is served by two public districts, Hazelwood and Ferguson-Florissant, so the school assignment on a given street matters. McCluer High School and McCluer North High School belong to Ferguson-Florissant, and North Technical High School is also in the city. Hazelwood Northwest Middle School and several elementary schools stand inside city limits. Parochial schools include St. Ferdinand, Sacred Heart and Saint Norbert.

Higher education is close by. Saint Louis Christian College is in Florissant, Lindenwood University runs its North County Campus in a former school building, and St. Louis Community College-Florissant Valley is nearby. Northwest HealthCare, an outpatient arm of Christian Hospital, operates a satellite of the Siteman Cancer Center on its campus.

Old Town draws a different buyer. It holds Missouri German brick buildings such as the Kuehn House, French wood-frame homes and the Old St. Ferdinand Shrine, whose four buildings date from 1819, 1821, 1840 and 1888. The wider City of St. Ferdinand resource area covers about 156 city blocks and 124 historically significant properties built between 1790 and 1940. If your house sits inside those blocks, ask the city whether exterior changes need review before you make repairs.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Florissant house without a city inspection?
faqs.a: Yes. The city lets a house sell as-is. Whoever buys it must obtain the inspection and occupancy permit before anyone moves in, which puts that step on the buyer's timeline.

faqs.q: Who records the deed after a Florissant sale?
faqs.a: The St. Louis County Recorder of Deeds, at 41 S Central Ave in Clayton. A standard deed costs $26 for the first page and $3 for each added page, plus $25 if the format is non-standard.

faqs.q: When does the county want Florissant property tax paid?
faqs.a: By December 31, either paid or postmarked that day. Anything later adds up to 18% interest per year and a 2% penalty under RSMo 139 and 140.

faqs.q: What happens to a Home Improvement Program loan if I sell?
faqs.a: It comes due. A sale within five years of the loan date requires repayment, and for a sale the city's program packet says repayment happens at closing. Call 314-839-7680 for the balance.
Federal estimates put the city at 51,124 residents in mid-2025, 2.7% below the 52,537 used as the 2020 base. The 1970 census counted 65,908.
